title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
event_hint: Empirical comparison of Semantic search (vector index + ReAct) vs Deep Agentic search (grep-search by isolated subagent) for repository-level code QA on SWE-QA across four LLMs; finds Semantic more accurate and cheaper, with a large failure share of Deep Agentic at the planner->subagent hand-off.
problem: Code agents spend much of their effort locating the right code inside a repository, and two paradigms dominate current practice: Semantic search (retrieve code blocks from a pre-built vector index) and Deep Agentic search (a planning agent delegates exploration to a separate subagent working in an isolated context window, returning only a condensed result, to protect the main agent from context pollution/context rot). Recent code agents (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) have quickly adopted Deep Agentic search as 'good context engineering practice', but there was little empirical evidence on whether it actually produces better answers than indexed retrieval for repository-level code QA.
mechanism: Two agent architectures compared on the SWE-QA benchmark (Peng et al., 2026a; open-ended questions over whole Python repositories). Semantic: a ReAct agent (LangChain SWE-QA Agent harness) restricted to three tools from the original benchmark protocol (repository structure lookup, retrieval tool over a vector index built once per repository by chunking files and embedding chunks, and a file reader), with no shell/filesystem-write/planning tools. Deep Agentic: a Deep Agent (LangChain Deep Agents framework harness with its default toolset including planning, a virtual filesystem, and sub-agent delegation), in which a planning orchestrator delegates exploration to an isolated sub-agent that returns a condensed result. Each question answered in a fresh conversation thread (no cross-question contamination), only the targeted repository available, all execution traces (tool calls, planner steps, sub-agent actions, token accounting) recorded. Differences in tools between the two paradigms are treated as constitutive of the paradigms, not as a confound. Three research questions: RQ1 accuracy, RQ2 cost/efficiency, RQ3 behaviour/failure modes; plus a six-mechanism/five-symptom failure taxonomy coded from traces (with two-author inter-rater Cohen's kappa 0.86 symptom / 0.78 mechanism).

evidence.claim: On SWE-QA, Semantic search answered 65.2% of questions correctly vs 46.2% for Deep Agentic search (pooled headline), and Semantic produced each correct answer at less than half the cost of Deep Agentic.
evidence.value: 65.2% vs 46.2% Pass; Semantic <half the $/correct of Deep Agentic
evidence.condition: SWE-QA repository-level code QA benchmark, four LLMs (Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B), graded by LLM judge validated against human panel
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 1 (Abstract); PDF Page 15 (Table 3 master comparison)

evidence.claim: Per-model Pass-rate advantage for Semantic over Deep Agentic: +5.6pp (Gemini 2.5 Flash), +10.0pp (Gemini 2.5 Pro), +10.6pp (Qwen3-235B) and +49.6pp (Gemini 3 Flash); all four McNemar and all four Wilcoxon tests remained significant after FDR correction. Cliff's delta on score ~0.14 for the two Gemini 2.5 models, ~0.24 for Qwen3-235B, ~0.76 for Gemini 3 Flash.
evidence.condition: paired within-model comparison, SWE-QA, four LLMs, McNemar + Wilcoxon with FDR, Cliff's delta

evidence.claim: Deep Agentic search did not remove failures but introduced a new failure class: the single largest share of its failures, 41.8%, occurred at the planner-to-sub-agent hand-off (coordination breakdown), which is structurally impossible for the flat Semantic agent; the association between architecture and failure mechanism is very strong (chi-square 508.8 on 5 df, Cramer's V 0.56; even excluding the Deep-only mechanism, chi-square 147.2 on 4 df, Cramer's V 0.35).
evidence.value: 41.8% of Deep failures at hand-off; chi-square 508.8 df5 V=0.56 (147.2 df4 V=0.35 excluding Deep-only)
evidence.condition: failure taxonomy coded from recorded traces, SWE-QA, four LLMs

evidence.claim: Cost/efficiency per condition (Table 3) shows Deep Agentic consistently more expensive: e.g. Gemini 2.5 Flash $0.1868/q and 0.436 $/Pass for Deep vs $0.1029/q and 0.213 $/Pass for Semantic; Gemini 3 Flash Deep 0.858 $/Pass vs Semantic 0.179 $/Pass; Qwen3-235B Deep 0.291 $/Pass vs Semantic 0.012 $/Pass, with Deep using far more tokens and tool calls (e.g. Qwen3-235B: 761k in-tok / 40.1 tools Deep vs 34k in-tok / 3.5 tools Semantic).
evidence.value: Deep 0.436/1.526/0.858/0.291 $/Pass vs Semantic 0.213/1.048/0.179/0.012 $/Pass across the four LLMs
evidence.condition: SWE-QA, $ includes reasoning tokens billed at completion rate, prompt+completion token columns reported separately
evidence.source_locator: PDF Page 15 (Table 3 master comparison per condition)

evidence.claim: Judge validity: on a stratified sample of 800 answers (100 per condition), human-majority vs LLM-judge agreement was Cohen's kappa 0.74 (84.0% exact agreement) on the categorical verdict and Pearson r=0.83 / Spearman rho=0.81 / MAD 5.2 score points on the harmonized 0-100 score; human panel internal Fleiss' kappa 0.81.
evidence.value: human vs judge kappa 0.74 (84.0%); Pearson r=0.83; MAD 5.2; panel Fleiss' kappa 0.81
evidence.condition: stratified 800-answer sample, 100 per condition, three-class verdict + harmonized 0-100 score

evaluation_context: Benchmark: SWE-QA (Peng et al., 2026a), repository-level code QA over whole Python repositories, each question in a fresh thread with only the targeted repository available. Two architectures: ReAct + Semantic search (vector index over chunked files, three tools) vs Deep Agent + Deep Agentic search (planner + isolated sub-agent, default Deep Agents toolset with planning, virtual filesystem, sub-agent delegation). Four LLMs evaluated: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Gemini 3 Flash, Qwen3-235B. Grading: LLM judge validated against an independent three-rater human panel on 800 stratified answers. Cost accounting includes prompt+completion tokens with reasoning tokens billed at the completion rate (so $/q is not simply token count times list price). Failure taxonomy: six mechanisms (coordination breakdown, retrieval/localization miss, insufficient grounding, evidence misinterpreted, non-terminating loop, evidence-gathering failure) and five symptoms; two-author inter-rater Cohen's kappa 0.86 symptom / 0.78 mechanism, consensus-vs-automatic kappa 0.82.
limitations: The two agent action spaces are intentionally not identical (the tool difference is constitutive of the paradigms, not a confound the authors try to remove), so the comparison is paradigm-level, not a controlled single-variable ablation. SWE-QA targets read-only repository-level code QA over Python repositories that can be pre-indexed; results may not generalize to write/patch tasks, non-Python repos, or repos that cannot be indexed. The headline 65.2% vs 46.2% pools across four models of very different capability (Gemini 3 Flash alone shows a 49.6pp gap while the Gemini 2.5 pair shows ~5.6-10pp), so the pooled number overstates the typical gap. Cost columns exclude some token categories from the displayed token counts (reasoning tokens are billed but reported separately), so $/q is not derivable from the shown token columns. The LLM judge, despite strong human agreement, still has MAD 5.2 score points and lower agreement on Deep conditions (kappa 0.69) than Semantic (0.78).
project_relevance: Highly relevant and contrarian for the agent-acceleration card: it directly tests the now-popular Deep Agentic / grep-by-subagent design (adopted by Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) against indexed Semantic retrieval on a real repo-QA benchmark and finds Semantic retrieval both more accurate and roughly half the cost per correct answer, with the Deep design introducing a new silent failure mode (41.8% of its failures at the planner->subagent hand-off, often ending in fluent confident wrong answers). This is actionable for the project: for read-only repo questions that can be indexed, retrieval is the stronger and cheaper option, and the context-pollution protection of sub-agent delegation is not free. Caveat: the result is for QA, not for write/patch SWE-bench-style tasks, and the tool surfaces differ by design, so it complements (does not contradict) papers that show structural indices helping patch resolve.

evidence_gaps.question: Do the accuracy/cost conclusions hold for write/patch (SWE-bench-style) tasks and for non-Python repositories, or only for read-only Python repo QA?
